title: How to sign up for a virtual power plant—and decide whether you should
gist: Virtual power plants (VPPs) — networks of smart thermostats, EVs, home batteries and solar that utilities can throttle at peak demand — have scaled to 500+ US programs and roughly 4 million enrolled smart-thermostat households, with utilities and now data-center-hungry tech companies like Google increasingly treating aggregated consumer devices as a substitute for new grid capacity.

insights.claim: A smart thermostat VPP program typically pays an enrollment bonus of roughly $50 to $150 plus about $25 to $50 per year, according to EnergyHub CEO Seth Frader-Thompson.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Thermostat-based VPP payouts are small per-household but represent a low-cost, low-friction demand-response product utilities can scale broadly; useful benchmark for sizing VPP software/services revenue per enrolled device.
insights.quote: a smart thermostat program may offer an initial bonus of roughly $50 to $150, plus about $25 to $50 per year
insights.locator: Seth Frader-Thompson, CEO and cofounder of EnergyHub

insights.claim: Home battery and EV-based VPP participation can yield hundreds to thousands of dollars in annual savings per household, far more than thermostat-only programs.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: The payout gap creates a natural upsell/upgrade path from thermostats to batteries/EVs for VPP operators, and signals where utility procurement dollars concentrate as battery-to-grid programs scale.
insights.quote: home battery and EV devices could yield hundreds or thousands of dollars in annual savings
insights.locator: Seth Frader-Thompson, CEO and cofounder

insights.claim: The most expensive consumer devices — EVs and home batteries — generate the largest VPP savings, which creates an affordability barrier since lower-income households without those assets are effectively locked out of the biggest payouts.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: VPP economics currently favor wealthier, asset-owning households, implying equity/policy pressure and a potential market segment for financing or subsidy programs to widen participation and grid benefit.
insights.quote: The most expensive devices, namely EVs and home batteries, are often what yield the greatest savings, which adds a barrier to entry for those who cannot afford these products in the first place.
insights.locator: Decide whether the offer is worth it

insights.claim: VPP compensation is structured in varied, non-uniform forms — signup bonuses, gift cards, monthly bill credits, discounted thermostats, cheaper EV charging, annual performance payments, or 'export credits' for energy sent back to the grid.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Fragmented, non-standardized incentive design across programs is a friction point that favors aggregator platforms (like EnergyHub, ChargeScape) that can normalize and market offers across many utilities.
insights.locator: Decide whether the offer is worth it for you

insights.claim: As of 2023 there were already more than 500 VPP programs operating in the US, and the count has continued growing since then.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: 500+ programs signals VPPs have moved past pilot stage into a mainstream utility procurement tool, a maturing addressable market for DER management software vendors.
insights.quote: As of 2023, there were already more than 500 VPP programs operating in the US alone, and the number has only grown since
insights.locator: As of 2023

insights.claim: An estimated 4 million US households with smart thermostats were enrolled in a VPP program as of the prior year (2025).
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: 4 million enrolled households gives a concrete penetration benchmark for smart-thermostat VPP adoption, useful for sizing TAM and tracking growth rate in future reporting.
insights.quote: An estimated 4 million households with smart thermostats were enrolled in a VPP program as of last year.
insights.locator: As of 2023

insights.claim: Big technology companies, notably Google, are starting to invest in VPP technology specifically to help power their data centers.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler investment in VPPs signals a new demand-side driver beyond residential bill savings — AI-driven data center power needs are pulling tech capital into distributed energy resource aggregation, a potential growth catalyst for VPP/DER platform vendors.
insights.quote: especially with big players like Google starting to invest in this technology to help power their data centers
insights.locator: As of 2023, there were already more than 500 VPP programs

insights.claim: Aggregated small per-household load reductions become materially significant at scale — EnergyHub's CEO likens hundreds of thousands to millions of participating devices to 'firing up a power plant.'
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: This is the core VPP value proposition for investors: distributed, low-cost residential flexibility can substitute for capital-intensive peaker plant or grid infrastructure buildout at sufficient scale.
insights.quote: When you put it together at the scale of hundreds of thousands, or millions, it has a pretty profound impact”, he says, equivalent to “firing up a power plant.
insights.locator: The amount of power the utility might throttle

insights.claim: Most consumer VPPs today only reduce or shift device load rather than actively export stored energy from EVs or home batteries back to the grid, but battery-to-grid programs are on the rise and could offer larger future consumer savings.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Bidirectional battery-to-grid (V2G/vehicle-to-grid and home-battery export) is flagged as the next growth vector in VPP economics, worth monitoring for inverter/hardware and software enablement plays.
insights.quote: But battery-to-grid programs are on the rise—and potentially offer even larger savings for consumers in the future.
insights.locator: Most consumer VPPs today are less dramatic

themes.theme: Grid reliability and program design risk

insights.claim: Poorly implemented VPP programs risk utilities mispredicting participant usage and paying them for energy reductions they never would have used anyway, which can raise energy bills for non-participating customers.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: A design/measurement flaw in baseline estimation is a real cost risk that could draw regulatory scrutiny or rate-case pushback, a factor for evaluating utility VPP program quality and regulatory risk.
insights.quote: a utility may incorrectly predict when VPP participants plan to use more electricity and pay them for not using energy they weren’t planning to use anyway, potentially increasing energy bills for nonparticipants
insights.locator: But the approach is still new

insights.claim: Well-designed VPP programs can help utilities avoid expensive grid upgrades or emergency power-conservation measures, according to UC Berkeley's Severin Borenstein.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
entities: UC Berkeley Energy Institute at Haas
insights.so_what: This is the capex-avoidance thesis for VPPs: aggregated demand flexibility as a substitute for peaker plants/grid capex, a key argument for utility capital allocation toward DER programs over traditional infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: if we do it well, I think it can really be a benefit
insights.locator: if a program is not implemented well

insights.claim: VPP programs are concentrated geographically in places with flexible-device penetration, stressed grids, supportive utilities, or strong state policy — specifically California, Texas, New England, and increasingly the mid-Atlantic.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Geographic concentration maps the near-term addressable market for VPP operators and utility partners, and flags where state policy and grid stress are driving adoption ahead of a national rollout.
insights.quote: Most programs are established in places with lots of flexible devices, stressed grids, supportive utilities, or strong state policies—especially California, Texas, New England, and increasingly parts of the mid-Atlantic region.
insights.locator: These programs are also not evenly distributed

insights.claim: Most consumers discover and enroll in VPP programs through the device manufacturer's app or channel rather than directly via the utility, per EnergyHub's CEO.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Device manufacturers (thermostat, EV, battery brands) function as the primary customer-acquisition channel for VPP enrollment, positioning OEM app ecosystems as a strategic gatekeeper/partner for utilities and aggregators.
insights.quote: The way most people actually learn about this and sign up is through the manufacturer of the device they have.
insights.locator: But don’t stop with the utility

insights.claim: EV drivers can often see VPP program terms and payment directly in their automaker's app and enroll with a single click, according to ChargeScape CEO Joseph Vellone.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Frictionless in-app enrollment via automaker platforms suggests EV VPP participation could scale faster than thermostat/battery programs that require third-party enrollment steps.
insights.quote: with a click of a button
insights.locator: EV drivers may be able to see the terms

insights.claim: Eligibility for VPP programs is narrowly device-specific: thermostat programs may require an approved Wi-Fi thermostat model, EV programs depend on automaker/charger/utility territory/rate plan, and battery programs depend on battery brand, inverter, or installer and whether the system can communicate with the utility.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Narrow interoperability requirements create fragmentation and switching costs, favoring hardware/software vendors that achieve broad utility and OEM certification/integration as a competitive moat.
insights.quote: Eligibility can get annoyingly specific.
insights.locator: Eligibility can get annoyingly specific

insights.claim: Some households lack the flexibility to participate in VPP programs at all — night-shift workers, people with caregiving or health needs, and those already minimizing energy use to save money may have little room to let a utility adjust their heating, cooling, or charging schedules.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: This flags an equity/adoption ceiling for VPP programs — a segment of the population structurally cannot participate, which limits total addressable enrollment and should temper aggressive VPP market-penetration forecasts.
insights.quote: do not have the flexibility to engage in one of these programs
insights.locator: Other households, however

insights.claim: For low-effort adopters, such as an EV that sits plugged in overnight but only needs two hours to charge, shifting charging time for a VPP program can be nearly invisible to the household.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Overnight EV charging is a low-friction, high-fit use case for managed-charging VPP programs, suggesting EV charging flexibility is an easier initial wedge for utility demand-response programs than other device categories.
insights.locator: If your EV sits plugged in all night

insights.claim: The right to 'opt out' of a temporary utility-initiated adjustment (e.g., skip a thermostat change, force immediate EV charging, preserve battery reserve) is what makes VPP programs workable for many customers, and utilities are generally motivated to keep the opt-out process simple.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Opt-out simplicity is a key trust/retention lever for VPP programs — investors evaluating VPP operators should weigh how frictionless override mechanisms are, since poor opt-out design likely drives churn and consumer distrust.
insights.quote: This right to “opt out” is what makes them workable for many customers.
insights.locator: VPP programs generally give participants

insights.claim: The Electronic Frontier Foundation has warned that VPP device data (EV charging status/schedule, thermostat usage patterns revealing when people are home, sleeping, or using appliances) could be used to infer private household routines and may be distributed beyond the utility to device manufacturers, software platforms, or third parties.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Data privacy is a latent regulatory and reputational risk for VPP operators; investors should watch for privacy-related regulation or opt-in requirements that could raise compliance costs or slow enrollment growth.
insights.quote: this data could be used to infer private routines inside a home
insights.locator: The Electronic Frontier Foundation

insights.claim: VPP operators ChargeScape and EnergyHub counter privacy concerns by stating the data they collect is limited and functional, focused on device-level physics/energy data and aggregate (not individual) customer behavior.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: Operators' privacy-minimization stance is a competitive/regulatory positioning point likely to matter as consumer data scrutiny of connected-home and EV programs increases.
insights.quote: It doesn’t really matter what any one customer is doing. It matters what the average customer is doing.
insights.locator: ChargeScape and Energy Hub say

insights.claim: EnergyHub's CEO frames VPP participation as one of the few directly effective consumer actions that simultaneously supports grid decarbonization, affordability, and reliability while paying the participant.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: This is the marketing/value narrative VPP operators use to drive enrollment beyond pure bill savings — investors should note that mission-driven framing (decarbonization, reliability) is being used alongside financial incentives to expand the addressable customer base.
insights.quote: There are not that many things that you can do that directly contribute to decarbonizing the electric supply, or to improving affordability, or to improving reliability, and this is just a clearly effective way to do that
insights.locator: You might have a variety of reasons

insights.claim: The article concludes that the best VPP program for a consumer is not necessarily the highest-paying one but the one that is clearest about what it controls, how much it pays, how easy opt-out is, and how well it supports community energy goals.
insights.speaker: Eshan Raul
insights.so_what: This transparency-over-payout framework suggests program design and communication quality, not just incentive size, will differentiate winning VPP operators in a maturing, increasingly competitive market.
insights.quote: the best VPP program is not necessarily the one that pays the most
insights.locator: In short, the best VPP program
